```text
CodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\sim}$20\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical trace inputs (mean 1{,}174 vs.\ 978 tokens), reducing the verdict label's share of the training loss to ${\sim}$0.085\%.
Under standard next-token loss, the model allocates the vast majority of gradient updates to predicting trace tokens rather than learning the verdict classification boundary.
This tokenizer-driven dilution is invisible at short trace budgets (tail-256/512), where CodeLlama performs comparably to other models (77.9\% and 98.2\%, respectively), but is expected to compound at longer budgets (1{,}024+ tokens) where trace tokens dominate the loss landscape.

This finding highlights tokenizer efficiency as a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training: architectures with less efficient tokenizers require adapted training strategies (e.g., label-only loss) to prevent the diagnostic signal from being drowned by trace token prediction.&lt;/tool_use_error>
```

```text
52	On this task, exception-only accuracy is \emph{signal-limited} rather than \emph{capacity-limited}: three architecture families spanning 1.5B to 13B converge on the same floor, while \texttt{no\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\% $\to$ 75.1\% $\to$ 76.5\%).
53	
54	\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency and training dynamics.}
55	CodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\sim}$20\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical trace inputs (mean 1{,}174 vs.\ 978 tokens), reducing the verdict label's share of the training loss to ${\sim}$0.085\%.
56	Under standard next-token loss, the model allocates the vast majority of gradient updates to predicting trace tokens rather than learning the verdict classification boundary.
57	This tokenizer-driven dilution is invisible at short trace budgets (tail-256/512), where CodeLlama performs comparably to other models (77.9\% and 98.2\%, respectively), but is expected to compound at longer budgets (1{,}024+ tokens) where trace tokens dominate the loss landscape.
58	A label-only loss variant (computing loss only on the verdict token, masking all trace positions) addresses this by decoupling verdict learning from trace prediction.
59	Under label-only loss, CodeLlama recovers to 98.2\% at tail-1024, matching other models; however, tail-2048 collapses to 41.8\%, indicating LoRA long-sequence instability under this regime (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
60	This finding highlights tokenizer efficiency as a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training: architectures with less efficient tokenizers require adapted training strategies (e.g., label-only loss) to prevent the diagnostic signal from being drowned by trace token prediction.
61	
62	\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}
63	The two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\geq}$99\%; Tier~2 = 86.1\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.
64	First, it implies a \emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may degrade performance through attention dilution.
65	Second, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised. Even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).
66	Third, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (median 150 tokens vs.\ ${\sim}$1{,}900 for VOTA post-truncation) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).
67	
68	\paragraph{Practical applications.}
69	Test frameworks report pass/fail, but ML-based verdict prediction adds value in three settings: (1)~\emph{patch correctness prediction}, where a verdict model predicts from a partial test trace whether a candidate patch fixes a bug without running the full suite; (2)~\emph{flaky test detection}, where trace-based prediction identifies likely-flaky outcomes across runs; and (3)~\emph{offline trace analysis}, where logged production traces enable retrospective quality assessment without re-execution.
70
```

```json
  "old_string": "\\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency and training dynamics.}\nCodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\\sim}$20\\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical trace inputs (mean 1{,}174 vs.\\ 978 tokens), reducing the verdict label's share of the training loss to ${\\sim}$0.085\\%.\nUnder standard next-token loss, the model allocates the vast majority of gradient updates to predicting trace tokens rather than learning the verdict classification boundary.\nThis tokenizer-driven dilution is invisible at short trace budgets (tail-256/512), where CodeLlama performs comparably to other models (77.9\\% and 98.2\\%, respectively), but is expected to compound at longer budgets (1{,}024+ tokens) where trace tokens dominate the loss landscape.\nA label-only loss variant (computing loss only on the verdict token, masking all trace positions) addresses this by decoupling verdict learning from trace prediction.\nUnder label-only loss, CodeLlama recovers to 98.2\\% at tail-1024, matching other models; however, tail-2048 collapses to 41.8\\%, indicating LoRA long-sequence instability under this regime (Appendix~\\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).\nThis finding highlights tokenizer efficiency as a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training: architectures with less efficient tokenizers require adapted training strategies (e.g., label-only loss) to prevent the diagnostic signal from being drowned by trace token prediction.",
```

```text
30	
31	\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}
32	Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models, with cross-architecture variance (42.44pp) dwarfing the SFT range (0.56pp).
33	The failure is not in exception detection but in verdict calibration: the model recognizes that an exception occurred but cannot reliably determine whether it terminated execution or was caught by a \texttt{try/except} block.
34	Performance does not correlate with model size: Qwen-1.5B (93.45\%) outperforms Qwen-7B (89.08\%) and CodeLlama-13B (51.01\%, extreme fail bias with 72.4\% of predictions as \texttt{fail}).
35	Within the Qwen family, the 1.5B model's higher zero-shot accuracy likely reflects consistent code training data quality across scales: the smaller model already understands exception format, but both lack the verdict-specific calibration that SFT provides (SFT gap: 6.38pp for 1.5B vs.\ 10.75pp for 7B).
36	Three-shot in-context learning (90.84\% on Qwen-7B, fail recall = 80.53\%) improves fail recall by 13.57pp over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp: three examples cannot cover the diversity of caught-exception patterns in the training distribution.
37	SFT normalizes this cross-architecture variance by grounding exception patterns in task-specific verdict labels, compressing a 42.44pp zero-shot range to 0.56pp.
38	
39	\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}
```

```json
    "oldString": "\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models, with cross-architecture variance (42.44pp) dwarfing the SFT range (0.56pp).\nThe failure is not in exception detection but in verdict calibration: the model recognizes that an exception occurred but cannot reliably determine whether it terminated execution or was caught by a \\texttt{try/except} block.\nPerformance does not correlate with model size: Qwen-1.5B (93.45\\%) outperforms Qwen-7B (89.08\\%) and CodeLlama-13B (51.01\\%, extreme fail bias with 72.4\\% of predictions as \\texttt{fail}).\nWithin the Qwen family, the 1.5B model's higher zero-shot accuracy likely reflects consistent code training data quality across scales: the smaller model already understands exception format, but both lack the verdict-specific calibration that SFT provides (SFT gap: 6.38pp for 1.5B vs.\\ 10.75pp for 7B).\nThree-shot in-context learning (90.84\\% on Qwen-7B, fail recall = 80.53\\%) improves fail recall by 13.57pp over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp: three examples cannot cover the diversity of caught-exception patterns in the training distribution.\nSFT normalizes this cross-architecture variance by grounding exception patterns in task-specific verdict labels, compressing a 42.44pp zero-shot range to 0.56pp.",
    "newString": "\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models (42.44pp range), while SFT compresses this to 0.56pp.\nThe bottleneck is verdict calibration, not exception detection: models recognize exceptions but cannot distinguish caught from uncaught ones.\nThree-shot ICL (90.84\\%) improves over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp, as three examples cannot cover caught-exception diversity.",
    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\nVerdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.\nException events succeed because they are the runtime's primary fault indicator.\nWhen Python raises an unhandled exception, it records exactly what went wrong (the error type), where it happened (the stack frame), and why (the error message).\nThis is precisely the information needed for a pass/fail decision, packaged in a compact, self-contained format.\nNon-exception trace components (variable states, loop iterations, line-by-line control flow) record \\emph{how} the program ran, not \\emph{whether} it failed, and dilute the model's attention without providing complementary diagnostic information.\n\nThis mechanistic account explains three key results.\nFirst, adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade accuracy (VOTA $<$ \\texttt{exception\\_only}, Table~\\ref{tab:ablation}), because non-diagnostic content competes for attention.\nSecond, a budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a phase transition localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens (\\S\\ref{sec:trace_length}).\nAt tail-384, all models remain near baseline (+1.0--6.5pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\\to$512 (+11.0--22.0pp), matching the typical exception traceback length (${\\sim}$400--500 tokens).\nBeyond this threshold, all models converge into a tight accuracy band regardless of scale or architecture, with \\texttt{tail\\_2048} capturing 95--98\\% of \\texttt{exception\\_only}'s accuracy.\nThis pattern confirms that the diagnostic signal is spatially concentrated: Python's error propagation records exceptions near the trace terminus, and the 384$\\to$512 token window is the critical boundary between signal capture and signal loss.\nThird, the 6.22pp SFT advantage over the best regex baseline concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}), confirming the model learns to distinguish \\emph{whether an exception terminated execution} rather than merely detecting exception presence.\nThe 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.\n\n\\paragraph{Why exception\\_only outperforms ae\\_only.}\nAlthough \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.92\\% on seed 42, it is a strict superset of the exception signal: assertion-point comparisons include the exception event (when present) plus additional information such as fallback local variable states.\nMulti-seed evaluation reveals that this extra content introduces noise: \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.64\\% mean accuracy ($\\pm$0.49, seeds 42/123/456) while \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves 99.83\\% ($\\pm$0.00).\nThe zero-variance result for \\texttt{exception\\_only} indicates that it captures a minimal sufficient signal (the compact exception event), while \\texttt{ae\\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) occasionally mislead the model, manifesting as seed-dependent variance ($\\sigma{=}$0.49pp).\nAttention analysis on representative samples confirms this interpretation: within exception events, the error type and location markers receive 5--10$\\times$ higher per-token attention than the verbose locals context (module paths, imported objects), suggesting the model learns to focus on diagnostic signals rather than incidental runtime state.\nThus \\texttt{exception\\_only} is both more precise and more stable than its superset.\n\n\\paragraph{SFT vs.\\ regex: semantic understanding.}\nThe primary evidence for learned semantic understanding comes from the nomarker ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}): with all format markers removed, SFT still achieves 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\\%).\nThis gap cannot be explained by format shortcuts and reflects genuine exception semantics learned through fine-tuning.\nAs auxiliary evidence, the B5-vs-SFT comparison (McNemar $p{=}0.041$, Table~\\ref{tab:regex}) shows that among 8 test samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions (from 2 distinct problems), SFT correctly classifies 6 (all from MBPP/113, a try/except ValueError pattern) while B5 misclassifies all 8.\nTogether, these results confirm that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions rather than merely detecting exception presence.\n\n\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models, with cross-architecture variance (42.44pp) dwarfing the SFT range (0.56pp).\nThe failure is not in exception detection but in verdict calibration: the model recognizes that an exception occurred but cannot reliably determine whether it terminated execution or was caught by a \\texttt{try/except} block.\nPerformance does not correlate with model size: Qwen-1.5B (93.45\\%) outperforms Qwen-7B (89.08\\%) and CodeLlama-13B (51.01\\%, extreme fail bias with 72.4\\% of predictions as \\texttt{fail}).\nWithin the Qwen family, the 1.5B model's higher zero-shot accuracy likely reflects consistent code training data quality across scales: the smaller model already understands exception format, but both lack the verdict-specific calibration that SFT provides (SFT gap: 6.38pp for 1.5B vs.\\ 10.75pp for 7B).\nThree-shot in-context learning (90.84\\% on Qwen-7B, fail recall = 80.53\\%) improves fail recall by 13.57pp over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp: three examples cannot cover the diversity of caught-exception patterns in the training distribution.\nSFT normalizes this cross-architecture variance by grounding exception patterns in task-specific verdict labels, compressing a 42.44pp zero-shot range to 0.56pp.\n\n\\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}\nThe B5 baseline (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}) achieves 99.33\\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker (\\texttt{[No exception data in trace]}) present in all pass samples.\nThis near-ceiling performance from a trivial pattern raises a concern: does SFT also learn this shortcut?\nThe answer is partially yes: the format marker correlates perfectly with the pass class. But the SFT model additionally handles the 8 boundary samples where exceptions occur in passing code, achieving 6/8 correct vs.\\ B5's 0/8.\nA \\emph{nomarker} ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) confirms genuine exception semantics: Qwen-7B 3-seed mean 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 and Qwen-1.5B 97.82\\%, a drop of only ${\\sim}$2pp.\nThe marker contribution (${\\sim}$9\\% of total lift) is small relative to semantic content (${\\sim}$91\\%), confirming that SFT learns exception semantics rather than format shortcuts.\nBoth signal layers show comparable accuracy across the two tested scales (1.5B and 7B produce 97.8\\% and 97.7\\% nomarker accuracy, respectively).\n\n\\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}\nSamples 901 and 905 (HumanEval/95, \\texttt{check\\_dict\\_case}) are misclassified by most configurations: Qwen-7B (3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B, and CodeLlama-13B seed 42/456 all produce exactly these 2 errors.\nThe root cause is deterministic: Python's \\texttt{all()} raises \\texttt{GeneratorExit} (a \\texttt{BaseException} subclass) during generator short-circuit, recorded as \\texttt{[ERROR]} despite the test passing.\nHowever, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\\% (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.\nThis confirms that 99.83\\% is a near-perfect \\emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most initializations) rather than a hard data limitation: the representation supports perfect accuracy, though most LoRA initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.\nOn this task, exception-only accuracy is \\emph{signal-limited} rather than \\emph{capacity-limited}: three architecture families spanning 1.5B to 13B converge on the same floor, while \\texttt{no\\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\\% $\\to$ 75.1\\% $\\to$ 76.5\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency.}\nCodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\\sim}$20\\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical inputs, reducing the verdict label's loss share to ${\\sim}$0.085\\%.\nA label-only loss variant recovers CodeLlama to 98.2\\% at tail-1024 but collapses at tail-2048 (41.8\\%), indicating LoRA long-sequence instability (Appendix~\\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).\nTokenizer efficiency is a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training.\n\n\\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}\nThe two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\\geq}$99\\%; Tier~2 = 86.1\\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.\nFirst, it implies a \\emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may degrade performance through attention dilution.\nSecond, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised. Even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).\nThird, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (median 150 tokens vs.\\ ${\\sim}$1{,}900 for VOTA post-truncation) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).\n\n\\paragraph{Practical applications.}\nTest frameworks report pass/fail, but ML-based verdict prediction adds value in three settings: (1)~\\emph{patch correctness prediction}, where a verdict model predicts from a partial test trace whether a candidate patch fixes a bug without running the full suite; (2)~\\emph{flaky test detection}, where trace-based prediction identifies likely-flaky outcomes across runs; and (3)~\\emph{offline trace analysis}, where logged production traces enable retrospective quality assessment without re-execution.\n",
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\nVerdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.\nException events succeed because they are the runtime's primary fault indicator.\nWhen Python raises an unhandled exception, it records exactly what went wrong (the error type), where it happened (the stack frame), and why (the error message).\nThis is precisely the information needed for a pass/fail decision, packaged in a compact, self-contained format.\nNon-exception trace components (variable states, loop iterations, line-by-line control flow) record \\emph{how} the program ran, not \\emph{whether} it failed, and dilute the model's attention without providing complementary diagnostic information.\n\nThis mechanistic account explains three key results.\nFirst, adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade accuracy (VOTA $<$ \\texttt{exception\\_only}, Table~\\ref{tab:ablation}), because non-diagnostic content competes for attention.\nSecond, a budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a phase transition localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens (\\S\\ref{sec:trace_length}).\nAt tail-384, all models remain near baseline (+1.0--6.5pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\\to$512 (+11.0--22.0pp), matching the typical exception traceback length (${\\sim}$400--500 tokens).\nBeyond this threshold, all models converge into a tight accuracy band regardless of scale or architecture, with \\texttt{tail\\_2048} capturing 95--98\\% of \\texttt{exception\\_only}'s accuracy.\nThis pattern confirms that the diagnostic signal is spatially concentrated: Python's error propagation records exceptions near the trace terminus, and the 384$\\to$512 token window is the critical boundary between signal capture and signal loss.\nThird, the 6.22pp SFT advantage over the best regex baseline concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}), confirming the model learns to distinguish \\emph{whether an exception terminated execution} rather than merely detecting exception presence.\nThe 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.\n\n\\paragraph{Why exception\\_only outperforms ae\\_only.}\nAlthough \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.92\\% on seed 42, it is a strict superset of the exception signal: assertion-point comparisons include the exception event (when present) plus additional information such as fallback local variable states.\nMulti-seed evaluation reveals that this extra content introduces noise: \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.64\\% mean accuracy ($\\pm$0.49, seeds 42/123/456) while \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves 99.83\\% ($\\pm$0.00).\nThe zero-variance result for \\texttt{exception\\_only} indicates that it captures a minimal sufficient signal (the compact exception event), while \\texttt{ae\\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) occasionally mislead the model, manifesting as seed-dependent variance ($\\sigma{=}$0.49pp).\nAttention analysis on representative samples confirms this interpretation: within exception events, the error type and location markers receive 5--10$\\times$ higher per-token attention than the verbose locals context (module paths, imported objects), suggesting the model learns to focus on diagnostic signals rather than incidental runtime state.\nThus \\texttt{exception\\_only} is both more precise and more stable than its superset.\n\n\\paragraph{SFT vs.\\ regex: semantic understanding.}\nThe primary evidence for learned semantic understanding comes from the nomarker ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}): with all format markers removed, SFT still achieves 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\\%).\nThis gap cannot be explained by format shortcuts and reflects genuine exception semantics learned through fine-tuning.\nAs auxiliary evidence, the B5-vs-SFT comparison (McNemar $p{=}0.041$, Table~\\ref{tab:regex}) shows that among 8 test samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions (from 2 distinct problems), SFT correctly classifies 6 (all from MBPP/113, a try/except ValueError pattern) while B5 misclassifies all 8.\nTogether, these results confirm that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions rather than merely detecting exception presence.\n\n\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models (42.44pp range), while SFT compresses this to 0.56pp.\nThe bottleneck is verdict calibration, not exception detection: models recognize exceptions but cannot distinguish caught from uncaught ones.\nThree-shot ICL (90.84\\%) improves over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp, as three examples cannot cover caught-exception diversity.\n\n\\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}\nThe B5 baseline (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}) achieves 99.33\\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker (\\texttt{[No exception data in trace]}) present in all pass samples.\nThis near-ceiling performance from a trivial pattern raises a concern: does SFT also learn this shortcut?\nThe answer is partially yes: the format marker correlates perfectly with the pass class. But the SFT model additionally handles the 8 boundary samples where exceptions occur in passing code, achieving 6/8 correct vs.\\ B5's 0/8.\nA \\emph{nomarker} ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) confirms genuine exception semantics: Qwen-7B 3-seed mean 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 and Qwen-1.5B 97.82\\%, a drop of only ${\\sim}$2pp.\nThe marker contribution (${\\sim}$9\\% of total lift) is small relative to semantic content (${\\sim}$91\\%), confirming that SFT learns exception semantics rather than format shortcuts.\nBoth signal layers show comparable accuracy across the two tested scales (1.5B and 7B produce 97.8\\% and 97.7\\% nomarker accuracy, respectively).\n\n\\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}\nSamples 901 and 905 (HumanEval/95, \\texttt{check\\_dict\\_case}) are misclassified by most configurations: Qwen-7B (3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B, and CodeLlama-13B seed 42/456 all produce exactly these 2 errors.\nThe root cause is deterministic: Python's \\texttt{all()} raises \\texttt{GeneratorExit} (a \\texttt{BaseException} subclass) during generator short-circuit, recorded as \\texttt{[ERROR]} despite the test passing.\nHowever, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\\% (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.\nThis confirms that 99.83\\% is a near-perfect \\emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most initializations) rather than a hard data limitation: the representation supports perfect accuracy, though most LoRA initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.\nOn this task, exception-only accuracy is \\emph{signal-limited} rather than \\emph{capacity-limited}: three architecture families spanning 1.5B to 13B converge on the same floor, while \\texttt{no\\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\\% $\\to$ 75.1\\% $\\to$ 76.5\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency.}\nCodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\\sim}$20\\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical inputs, reducing the verdict label's loss share to ${\\sim}$0.085\\%.\nA label-only loss variant recovers CodeLlama to 98.2\\% at tail-1024 but collapses at tail-2048 (41.8\\%), indicating LoRA long-sequence instability (Appendix~\\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).\nTokenizer efficiency is a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training.\n\n\\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}\nThe two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\\geq}$99\\%; Tier~2 = 86.1\\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.\nFirst, it implies a \\emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may degrade performance through attention dilution.\nSecond, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised. Even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).\nThird, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (median 150 tokens vs.\\ ${\\sim}$1{,}900 for VOTA post-truncation) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).\n\n\\paragraph{Practical applications.}\nTest frameworks report pass/fail, but ML-based verdict prediction adds value in three settings: (1)~\\emph{patch correctness prediction}, where a verdict model predicts from a partial test trace whether a candidate patch fixes a bug without running the full suite; (2)~\\emph{flaky test detection}, where trace-based prediction identifies likely-flaky outcomes across runs; and (3)~\\emph{offline trace analysis}, where logged production traces enable retrospective quality assessment without re-execution.\n",
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\nVerdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.\nException events succeed because they are the runtime's primary fault indicator.\nWhen Python raises an unhandled exception, it records exactly what went wrong (the error type), where it happened (the stack frame), and why (the error message).\nThis is precisely the information needed for a pass/fail decision, packaged in a compact, self-contained format.\nNon-exception trace components (variable states, loop iterations, line-by-line control flow) record \\emph{how} the program ran, not \\emph{whether} it failed, and dilute the model's attention without providing complementary diagnostic information.\n\nThis mechanistic account explains three key results.\nFirst, adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade accuracy (VOTA $<$ \\texttt{exception\\_only}, Table~\\ref{tab:ablation}), because non-diagnostic content competes for attention.\nSecond, a budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a phase transition localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens (\\S\\ref{sec:trace_length}).\nAt tail-384, all models remain near baseline (+1.0--6.5pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\\to$512 (+11.0--22.0pp), matching the typical exception traceback length (${\\sim}$400--500 tokens).\nBeyond this threshold, all models converge into a tight accuracy band regardless of scale or architecture, with \\texttt{tail\\_2048} capturing 95--98\\% of \\texttt{exception\\_only}'s accuracy.\nThis pattern confirms that the diagnostic signal is spatially concentrated: Python's error propagation records exceptions near the trace terminus, and the 384$\\to$512 token window is the critical boundary between signal capture and signal loss.\nThird, the 6.22pp SFT advantage over the best regex baseline concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}), confirming the model learns to distinguish \\emph{whether an exception terminated execution} rather than merely detecting exception presence.\nThe 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.\n\n\\paragraph{Why exception\\_only outperforms ae\\_only.}\nAlthough \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.92\\% on seed 42, it is a strict superset of the exception signal: assertion-point comparisons include the exception event (when present) plus additional information such as fallback local variable states.\nMulti-seed evaluation reveals that this extra content introduces noise: \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.64\\% mean accuracy ($\\pm$0.49, seeds 42/123/456) while \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves 99.83\\% ($\\pm$0.00).\nThe zero-variance result for \\texttt{exception\\_only} indicates that it captures a minimal sufficient signal (the compact exception event), while \\texttt{ae\\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) occasionally mislead the model, manifesting as seed-dependent variance ($\\sigma{=}$0.49pp).\nAttention analysis on representative samples confirms this interpretation: within exception events, the error type and location markers receive 5--10$\\times$ higher per-token attention than the verbose locals context (module paths, imported objects), suggesting the model learns to focus on diagnostic signals rather than incidental runtime state.\nThus \\texttt{exception\\_only} is both more precise and more stable than its superset.\n\n\\paragraph{SFT vs.\\ regex: semantic understanding.}\nThe primary evidence for learned semantic understanding comes from the nomarker ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}): with all format markers removed, SFT still achieves 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\\%).\nThis gap cannot be explained by format shortcuts and reflects genuine exception semantics learned through fine-tuning.\nAs auxiliary evidence, the B5-vs-SFT comparison (McNemar $p{=}0.041$, Table~\\ref{tab:regex}) shows that among 8 test samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions (from 2 distinct problems), SFT correctly classifies 6 (all from MBPP/113, a try/except ValueError pattern) while B5 misclassifies all 8.\nTogether, these results confirm that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions rather than merely detecting exception presence.\n\n\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models (42.44pp range), while SFT compresses this to 0.56pp.\nThe bottleneck is verdict calibration, not exception detection: models recognize exceptions but cannot distinguish caught from uncaught ones.\nThree-shot ICL (90.84\\%) improves over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp, as three examples cannot cover caught-exception diversity.\n\n\\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}\nA regex baseline (B5) achieves 99.33\\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker present in all pass samples, raising the concern that SFT learns this shortcut.\nA \\emph{nomarker} ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) resolves this: removing all markers drops accuracy by only ${\\sim}$2pp (Qwen-7B 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96, Qwen-1.5B 97.82\\%), and SFT correctly handles 6/8 boundary samples where caught exceptions occur in passing code (vs.\\ 0/8 for the regex).\nThe marker contribution (${\\sim}$9\\%) is small relative to semantic content (${\\sim}$91\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}\nSamples 901 and 905 (HumanEval/95, \\texttt{check\\_dict\\_case}) are misclassified by most configurations: Qwen-7B (3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B, and CodeLlama-13B seed 42/456 all produce exactly these 2 errors.\nThe root cause is deterministic: Python's \\texttt{all()} raises \\texttt{GeneratorExit} (a \\texttt{BaseException} subclass) during generator short-circuit, recorded as \\texttt{[ERROR]} despite the test passing.\nHowever, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\\% (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.\nThis confirms that 99.83\\% is a near-perfect \\emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most initializations) rather than a hard data limitation: the representation supports perfect accuracy, though most LoRA initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.\nOn this task, exception-only accuracy is \\emph{signal-limited} rather than \\emph{capacity-limited}: three architecture families spanning 1.5B to 13B converge on the same floor, while \\texttt{no\\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\\% $\\to$ 75.1\\% $\\to$ 76.5\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency.}\nCodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\\sim}$20\\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical inputs, reducing the verdict label's loss share to ${\\sim}$0.085\\%.\nA label-only loss variant recovers CodeLlama to 98.2\\% at tail-1024 but collapses at tail-2048 (41.8\\%), indicating LoRA long-sequence instability (Appendix~\\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).\nTokenizer efficiency is a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training.\n\n\\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}\nThe two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\\geq}$99\\%; Tier~2 = 86.1\\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.\nFirst, it implies a \\emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may degrade performance through attention dilution.\nSecond, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised. Even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).\nThird, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (median 150 tokens vs.\\ ${\\sim}$1{,}900 for VOTA post-truncation) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).\n\n\\paragraph{Practical applications.}\nTest frameworks report pass/fail, but ML-based verdict prediction adds value in three settings: (1)~\\emph{patch correctness prediction}, where a verdict model predicts from a partial test trace whether a candidate patch fixes a bug without running the full suite; (2)~\\emph{flaky test detection}, where trace-based prediction identifies likely-flaky outcomes across runs; and (3)~\\emph{offline trace analysis}, where logged production traces enable retrospective quality assessment without re-execution.\n",
```

```json
    "oldString": "\\paragraph{SFT vs.\\ regex: semantic understanding.}\nThe primary evidence for learned semantic understanding comes from the nomarker ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}): with all format markers removed, SFT still achieves 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\\%).\nThis gap cannot be explained by format shortcuts and reflects genuine exception semantics learned through fine-tuning.\nAs auxiliary evidence, the B5-vs-SFT comparison (McNemar $p{=}0.041$, Table~\\ref{tab:regex}) shows that among 8 test samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions (from 2 distinct problems), SFT correctly classifies 6 (all from MBPP/113, a try/except ValueError pattern) while B5 misclassifies all 8.\nTogether, these results confirm that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions rather than merely detecting exception presence.",

    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\nVerdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.\nException events succeed because they are the runtime's primary fault indicator.\nWhen Python raises an unhandled exception, it records exactly what went wrong (the error type), where it happened (the stack frame), and why (the error message).\nThis is precisely the information needed for a pass/fail decision, packaged in a compact, self-contained format.\nNon-exception trace components (variable states, loop iterations, line-by-line control flow) record \\emph{how} the program ran, not \\emph{whether} it failed, and dilute the model's attention without providing complementary diagnostic information.\n\nThis mechanistic account explains three key results.\nFirst, adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade accuracy (VOTA $<$ \\texttt{exception\\_only}, Table~\\ref{tab:ablation}), because non-diagnostic content competes for attention.\nSecond, a budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a phase transition localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens (\\S\\ref{sec:trace_length}).\nAt tail-384, all models remain near baseline (+1.0--6.5pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\\to$512 (+11.0--22.0pp), matching the typical exception traceback length (${\\sim}$400--500 tokens).\nBeyond this threshold, all models converge into a tight accuracy band regardless of scale or architecture, with \\texttt{tail\\_2048} capturing 95--98\\% of \\texttt{exception\\_only}'s accuracy.\nThis pattern confirms that the diagnostic signal is spatially concentrated: Python's error propagation records exceptions near the trace terminus, and the 384$\\to$512 token window is the critical boundary between signal capture and signal loss.\nThird, the 6.22pp SFT advantage over the best regex baseline concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}), confirming the model learns to distinguish \\emph{whether an exception terminated execution} rather than merely detecting exception presence.\nThe 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.\n\n\\paragraph{Why exception\\_only outperforms ae\\_only.}\nAlthough \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.92\\% on seed 42, it is a strict superset of the exception signal: assertion-point comparisons include the exception event (when present) plus additional information such as fallback local variable states.\nMulti-seed evaluation reveals that this extra content introduces noise: \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.64\\% mean accuracy ($\\pm$0.49, seeds 42/123/456) while \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves 99.83\\% ($\\pm$0.00).\nThe zero-variance result for \\texttt{exception\\_only} indicates that it captures a minimal sufficient signal (the compact exception event), while \\texttt{ae\\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) occasionally mislead the model, manifesting as seed-dependent variance ($\\sigma{=}$0.49pp).\nAttention analysis on representative samples confirms this interpretation: within exception events, the error type and location markers receive 5--10$\\times$ higher per-token attention than the verbose locals context (module paths, imported objects), suggesting the model learns to focus on diagnostic signals rather than incidental runtime state.\nThus \\texttt{exception\\_only} is both more precise and more stable than its superset.\n\n\\paragraph{SFT vs.\\ regex: semantic understanding.}\nThe primary evidence for learned semantic understanding comes from the nomarker ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}): with all format markers removed, SFT still achieves 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\\%).\nThis gap cannot be explained by format shortcuts and reflects genuine exception semantics learned through fine-tuning.\nAs auxiliary evidence, the B5-vs-SFT comparison (McNemar $p{=}0.041$, Table~\\ref{tab:regex}) shows that among 8 test samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions (from 2 distinct problems), SFT correctly classifies 6 (all from MBPP/113, a try/except ValueError pattern) while B5 misclassifies all 8.\nTogether, these results confirm that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions rather than merely detecting exception presence.\n\n\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models (42.44pp range), while SFT compresses this to 0.56pp.\nThe bottleneck is verdict calibration, not exception detection: models recognize exceptions but cannot distinguish caught from uncaught ones.\nThree-shot ICL (90.84\\%) improves over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp, as three examples cannot cover caught-exception diversity.\n\n\\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}\nA regex baseline (B5) achieves 99.33\\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker present in all pass samples, raising the concern that SFT learns this shortcut.\nA \\emph{nomarker} ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) resolves this: removing all markers drops accuracy by only ${\\sim}$2pp (Qwen-7B 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96, Qwen-1.5B 97.82\\%), and SFT correctly handles 6/8 boundary samples where caught exceptions occur in passing code (vs.\\ 0/8 for the regex).\nThe marker contribution (${\\sim}$9\\%) is small relative to semantic content (${\\sim}$91\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}\nThe 2 errors (samples 901/905, both \\texttt{GeneratorExit} from Python's \\texttt{all()} short-circuit) are shared across most configurations (Appendix~\\ref{sec:error_analysis}).\nCodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\\%, confirming that 99.83\\% is a convergence \\emph{floor}, not a data limitation.\nException-only accuracy is \\emph{signal-limited} rather than \\emph{capacity-limited}: three families (1.5B--13B) converge on the same floor, while \\texttt{no\\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\\% $\\to$ 75.1\\% $\\to$ 76.5\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency.}\nCodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\\sim}$20\\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical inputs, reducing the verdict label's loss share to ${\\sim}$0.085\\%.\nA label-only loss variant recovers CodeLlama to 98.2\\% at tail-1024 but collapses at tail-2048 (41.8\\%), indicating LoRA long-sequence instability (Appendix~\\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).\nTokenizer efficiency is a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training.\n\n\\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}\nThe two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\\geq}$99\\%; Tier~2 = 86.1\\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.\nFirst, it implies a \\emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may degrade performance through attention dilution.\nSecond, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised. Even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).\nThird, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (median 150 tokens vs.\\ ${\\sim}$1{,}900 for VOTA post-truncation) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).\n\n\\paragraph{Practical applications.}\nTest frameworks report pass/fail, but ML-based verdict prediction adds value in three settings: (1)~\\emph{patch correctness prediction}, where a verdict model predicts from a partial test trace whether a candidate patch fixes a bug without running the full suite; (2)~\\emph{flaky test detection}, where trace-based prediction identifies likely-flaky outcomes across runs; and (3)~\\emph{offline trace analysis}, where logged production traces enable retrospective quality assessment without re-execution.\n",
```

```text
24	Our exception-based approach and SBFL share the principle that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal, but operate at different granularities: we classify at the test level (pass/fail) while FL localizes at the statement or method level.
25	
26	\paragraph{Trace Compression and Selection.}
27	TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction for debugging; RepairAgent \citep{bouzenia2025repairagent} incorporates execution feedback in an autonomous repair loop.
28	\citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit, supporting our compression finding.
29	SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench} provides a realistic benchmark for code agents that must reason about test execution.
30	Our approximate information density decomposition (gradient dilution ${\sim}$26\% vs.\ information overload ${\sim}$74\%) provides the first quantitative framework for \emph{why} compression helps, complementing these methods' focus on \emph{how} to compress.
31	
32	\paragraph{Calibration and Defect Prediction.}
33	LLM calibration \citep{kadavath2022language,spiess2025calibration} measures whether model confidence aligns with actual correctness; our finding that \texttt{exception\_only} achieves ECE ${<}$ 0.007 across three architectures suggests that compact, high-specificity inputs improve calibration.
34	Just-in-time defect prediction \citep{kamei2013large} shares our motivation of early fault detection, though it operates on code change features rather than execution traces.
35	
```

```json
    "oldString": "\\paragraph{Calibration and Defect Prediction.}\nLLM calibration \\citep{kadavath2022language,spiess2025calibration} measures whether model confidence aligns with actual correctness; our finding that \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves ECE ${<}$ 0.007 across three architectures suggests that compact, high-specificity inputs improve calibration.\nJust-in-time defect prediction \\citep{kamei2013large} shares our motivation of early fault detection, though it operates on code change features rather than execution traces.",
    "newString": "\\paragraph{Calibration and Defect Prediction.}\nLLM calibration research \\citep{kadavath2022language,spiess2025calibration} studies confidence-correctness alignment; our ECE ${<}$ 0.007 finding suggests compact inputs improve calibration.\nJust-in-time defect prediction \\citep{kamei2013large} shares our early fault detection motivation but operates on code change features rather than execution traces.",
    "originalFile": "\\section{Related Work}\n\n\\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code LLMs.}\nTracePile \\citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples; \\citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility to be task- and format-dependent, a finding we extend by identifying exception events as the dominant signal for verdict prediction.\nNExT \\citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \\citep{eguchi2025etcot} leveraged trace chain-of-thought for repair and execution reasoning.\n\\citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, supporting our information density finding.\n\\citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained on execution traces for code understanding, and \\citet{chen2024selfdebug} demonstrated that LLMs can self-debug by reasoning over execution results.\nCRUXEval \\citep{gu2024cruxeval} established execution reasoning benchmarks, extended to 19 languages by \\citet{xu2025cruxevalx}.\nNone decompose which trace components contribute to \\emph{classification} accuracy.\n\n\\paragraph{Code Verdict and Patch Classification.}\nTRACED \\citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability and clone detection; DeepDFA \\citep{steenhoek2024deepdfa} combined dataflow analysis with deep learning for vulnerability detection.\nIn patch correctness, \\citet{tian2020patchcorrectness} pioneered representation learning of code changes; APPT \\citep{appt2024} achieved 79.7\\% with BERT+LSTM; LLM4PatchCorrect \\citep{zhou2024llm4patch} reached 84.4\\% using execution traces.\nTOGA \\citep{dinella2022toga} generated test oracles from execution information.\nFuseFL \\citep{widyasari2024fusefl} demonstrated that structured fault signals improve fault localization.\n\\citet{foster2025mutation} deployed LLM-based equivalence detection at Meta with 0.95 precision.\nThese approaches treat traces as monolithic inputs; none isolate individual components, compare against rule-based baselines to quantify the value of learned representations, or test cross-model generalization.\n\n\\paragraph{Fault Localization.}\nSpectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) ranks program elements by statistical suspiciousness computed from passing/failing test spectra.\nClassic metrics (Ochiai \\citep{abreu2007accuracy}, Tarantula \\citep{jones2002visualization}, DStar \\citep{wong2014dstar}) share a core insight with our work: abnormal execution events (here, coverage patterns correlated with failure) are the most informative diagnostic signal.\nRecent LLM-based approaches extend this: AutoFL \\citep{kang2024autofl} uses function-level call graphs with ChatGPT; AgentFL \\citep{qin2024agentfl} introduces multi-agent localization; LLM4FL \\citep{widyasari2024llm4fl} combines SBFL spectra with LLM reasoning; and \\citet{mukherjee2025llmfl} demonstrate that LLMs can localize faults from test failure information alone.\nVerdict prediction is a prerequisite to fault localization: one must first determine \\emph{whether} a fault exists before localizing \\emph{where} it is.\nOur exception-based approach and SBFL share the principle that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal, but operate at different granularities: we classify at the test level (pass/fail) while FL localizes at the statement or method level.\n\n\\paragraph{Trace Compression and Selection.}\nTraceCoder \\citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \\citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction for debugging; RepairAgent \\citep{bouzenia2025repairagent} incorporates execution feedback in an autonomous repair loop.\n\\citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit, supporting our compression finding.\nSWE-bench \\citep{jimenez2024swebench} provides a realistic benchmark for code agents that must reason about test execution.\nOur approximate information density decomposition (gradient dilution ${\\sim}$26\\% vs.\\ information overload ${\\sim}$74\\%) provides the first quantitative framework for \\emph{why} compression helps, complementing these methods' focus on \\emph{how} to compress.\n\n\\paragraph{Calibration and Defect Prediction.}\nLLM calibration \\citep{kadavath2022language,spiess2025calibration} measures whether model confidence aligns with actual correctness; our finding that \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves ECE ${<}$ 0.007 across three architectures suggests that compact, high-specificity inputs improve calibration.\nJust-in-time defect prediction \\citep{kamei2013large} shares our motivation of early fault detection, though it operates on code change features rather than execution traces.\n",
```

```text
16	The 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.
17	
18	\paragraph{Why exception\_only outperforms ae\_only.}
19	Although \texttt{ae\_only} achieves 99.92\% on seed 42, it is a strict superset of the exception signal: assertion-point comparisons include the exception event (when present) plus additional information such as fallback local variable states.
20	Multi-seed evaluation reveals that this extra content introduces noise: \texttt{ae\_only} achieves 99.64\% mean accuracy ($\pm$0.49, seeds 42/123/456) while \texttt{exception\_only} achieves 99.83\% ($\pm$0.00).
21	The zero-variance result for \texttt{exception\_only} indicates that it captures a minimal sufficient signal (the compact exception event), while \texttt{ae\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) occasionally mislead the model, manifesting as seed-dependent variance ($\sigma{=}$0.49pp).
22	Attention analysis on representative samples confirms this interpretation: within exception events, the error type and location markers receive 5--10$\times$ higher per-token attention than the verbose locals context (module paths, imported objects), suggesting the model learns to focus on diagnostic signals rather than incidental runtime state.
23	Thus \texttt{exception\_only} is both more precise and more stable than its superset.
24	
25	\paragraph{SFT vs.\ regex: semantic understanding.}
26	The nomarker ablation (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}) provides the primary evidence: with all format markers removed, SFT achieves 97.65\%$\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\%).
27	On the 8 boundary samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions, SFT correctly classifies 6/8 while the regex misclassifies all 8 (McNemar $p{=}0.041$), confirming that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions.
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\nVerdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.\nException events succeed because they are the runtime's primary fault indicator.\nWhen Python raises an unhandled exception, it records exactly what went wrong (the error type), where it happened (the stack frame), and why (the error message).\nThis is precisely the information needed for a pass/fail decision, packaged in a compact, self-contained format.\nNon-exception trace components (variable states, loop iterations, line-by-line control flow) record \\emph{how} the program ran, not \\emph{whether} it failed, and dilute the model's attention without providing complementary diagnostic information.\n\nThis mechanistic account explains three key results.\nFirst, adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade accuracy (VOTA $<$ \\texttt{exception\\_only}, Table~\\ref{tab:ablation}), because non-diagnostic content competes for attention.\nSecond, a budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a phase transition localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens (\\S\\ref{sec:trace_length}).\nAt tail-384, all models remain near baseline (+1.0--6.5pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\\to$512 (+11.0--22.0pp), matching the typical exception traceback length (${\\sim}$400--500 tokens).\nBeyond this threshold, all models converge into a tight accuracy band regardless of scale or architecture, with \\texttt{tail\\_2048} capturing 95--98\\% of \\texttt{exception\\_only}'s accuracy.\nThis pattern confirms that the diagnostic signal is spatially concentrated: Python's error propagation records exceptions near the trace terminus, and the 384$\\to$512 token window is the critical boundary between signal capture and signal loss.\nThird, the 6.22pp SFT advantage over the best regex baseline concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}), confirming the model learns to distinguish \\emph{whether an exception terminated execution} rather than merely detecting exception presence.\nThe 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.\n\n\\paragraph{Why exception\\_only outperforms ae\\_only.}\nAlthough \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.92\\% on seed 42, it is a strict superset of the exception signal: assertion-point comparisons include the exception event (when present) plus additional information such as fallback local variable states.\nMulti-seed evaluation reveals that this extra content introduces noise: \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.64\\% mean accuracy ($\\pm$0.49, seeds 42/123/456) while \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves 99.83\\% ($\\pm$0.00).\nThe zero-variance result for \\texttt{exception\\_only} indicates that it captures a minimal sufficient signal (the compact exception event), while \\texttt{ae\\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) occasionally mislead the model, manifesting as seed-dependent variance ($\\sigma{=}$0.49pp).\nAttention analysis on representative samples confirms this interpretation: within exception events, the error type and location markers receive 5--10$\\times$ higher per-token attention than the verbose locals context (module paths, imported objects), suggesting the model learns to focus on diagnostic signals rather than incidental runtime state.\nThus \\texttt{exception\\_only} is both more precise and more stable than its superset.\n\n\\paragraph{SFT vs.\\ regex: semantic understanding.}\nThe nomarker ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) provides the primary evidence: with all format markers removed, SFT achieves 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\\%).\nOn the 8 boundary samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions, SFT correctly classifies 6/8 while the regex misclassifies all 8 (McNemar $p{=}0.041$), confirming that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions.\n\n\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models (42.44pp range), while SFT compresses this to 0.56pp.\nThe bottleneck is verdict calibration, not exception detection: models recognize exceptions but cannot distinguish caught from uncaught ones.\nThree-shot ICL (90.84\\%) improves over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp, as three examples cannot cover caught-exception diversity.\n\n\\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}\nA regex baseline (B5) achieves 99.33\\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker present in all pass samples, raising the concern that SFT learns this shortcut.\nA \\emph{nomarker} ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) resolves this: removing all markers drops accuracy by only ${\\sim}$2pp (Qwen-7B 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96, Qwen-1.5B 97.82\\%), and SFT correctly handles 6/8 boundary samples where caught exceptions occur in passing code (vs.\\ 0/8 for the regex).\nThe marker contribution (${\\sim}$9\\%) is small relative to semantic content (${\\sim}$91\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}\nThe 2 errors (samples 901/905, both \\texttt{GeneratorExit} from Python's \\texttt{all()} short-circuit) are shared across most configurations (Appendix~\\ref{sec:error_analysis}).\nCodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\\%, confirming that 99.83\\% is a convergence \\emph{floor}, not a data limitation.\nException-only accuracy is \\emph{signal-limited} rather than \\emph{capacity-limited}: three families (1.5B--13B) converge on the same floor, while \\texttt{no\\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\\% $\\to$ 75.1\\% $\\to$ 76.5\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency.}\nCodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\\sim}$20\\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical inputs, reducing the verdict label's loss share to ${\\sim}$0.085\\%.\nA label-only loss variant recovers CodeLlama to 98.2\\% at tail-1024 but collapses at tail-2048 (41.8\\%), indicating LoRA long-sequence instability (Appendix~\\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).\nTokenizer efficiency is a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training.\n\n\\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}\nThe two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\\geq}$99\\%; Tier~2 = 86.1\\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.\nFirst, it implies a \\emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may degrade performance through attention dilution.\nSecond, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised. Even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).\nThird, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (median 150 tokens vs.\\ ${\\sim}$1{,}900 for VOTA post-truncation) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).\n\n\\paragraph{Practical applications.}\nTest frameworks report pass/fail, but ML-based verdict prediction adds value in three settings: (1)~\\emph{patch correctness prediction}, where a verdict model predicts from a partial test trace whether a candidate patch fixes a bug without running the full suite; (2)~\\emph{flaky test detection}, where trace-based prediction identifies likely-flaky outcomes across runs; and (3)~\\emph{offline trace analysis}, where logged production traces enable retrospective quality assessment without re-execution.\n",
```

```text
15	The 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\nVerdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.\nException events succeed (the error message).\nThis is precisely the information needed for a pass/fail decision, packaged in a compact, self-contained format.\nNon-exception trace components (variable states, loop iterations, line-by-line control flow) record \\emph{how} the program ran, not \\emph{whether} it failed, and dilute the model's attention without providing complementary diagnostic information.\n\nThis mechanistic account explains three key results.\nFirst, adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade accuracy (VOTA $<$ \\texttt{exception\\_only}, Table~\\ref{tab:ablation}), because non-diagnostic content competes for attention.\nSecond, a budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a best regex baseline concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}), confirming the model learns to distinguish \\emph{whether an exception terminated execution} rather than merely detecting exception presence.\nThe 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.\n\n\\paragraph{Why exception\\_only outperforms ae\\_only.}\nAlthough \\texttt{ae\\_only} is a strict superset of the exception signal, multi-seed evaluation reveals that the extra content introduces noise: \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.64\\%$\\pm$0.49 while \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves 99.83\\%$\\pm$0.00.\nThe zero-variance result indicates that \\texttt{exception\\_only} captures a minimal sufficient signal, while \\texttt{ae\\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) introduce seed-dependent variance.\n\n\\paragraph{SFT vs.\\ regex: semantic understanding.}\nThe nomarker ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) provides the primary evidence: with all format markers removed, SFT achieves 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\\%).\nOn the 8 boundary samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions, SFT correctly classifies 6/8 while the regex misclassifies all 8 (McNemar $p{=}0.041$), confirming that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions.\n\n\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models (42.44pp range), while SFT compresses this to 0.56pp.\nThe bottleneck is verdict calibration, not exception detection: models recognize exceptions but cannot distinguish caught from uncaught ones.\nThree-shot ICL (90.84\\%) improves over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp, as three examples cannot cover caught-exception diversity.\n\n\\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}\nA regex baseline (B5) achieves 99.33\\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker present in all pass samples, raising the concern that SFT learns this shortcut.\nA \\emph{nomarker} ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) resolves this: removing all markers drops accuracy by only ${\\sim}$2pp (Qwen-7B 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96, Qwen-1.5B 97.82\\%), and SFT correctly handles 6/8 boundary samples where caught exceptions occur in passing code (vs.\\ 0/8 for the regex).\nThe marker contribution (${\\sim}$9\\%) is small relative to semantic content (${\\sim}$91\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}\nThe 2 errors (samples 901/905, both \\texttt{GeneratorExit} from Python's \\texttt{all()} short-circuit) are shared across most configurations (Appendix~\\ref{sec:error_analysis}).\nCodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\\%, confirming that 99.83\\% is a convergence \\emph{floor}, not a data limitation.\nException-only accuracy is \\emph{signal-limited} rather than \\emph{capacity-limited}: three families (1.5B--13B) converge on the same floor, while \\texttt{no\\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\\% $\\to$ 75.1\\% $\\to$ 76.5\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency.}\nCodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\\sim}$20\\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical inputs, reducing the verdict label's loss share to ${\\sim}$0.085\\%.\nA label-only loss variant recovers CodeLlama to 98.2\\% at tail-1024 but collapses at tail-2048 (41.8\\%), indicating LoRA long-sequence instability (Appendix~\\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).\nTokenizer efficiency is a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training.\n\n\\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}\nThe two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\\geq}$99\\%; Tier~2 = 86.1\\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.\nFirst, it implies a \\emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may degrade performance through attention dilution.\nSecond, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised. Even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).\nThird, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (median 150 tokens vs.\\ ${\\sim}$1{,}900 for VOTA post-truncation) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).\n\n\\paragraph{Practical applications.}\nTest frameworks report pass/fail, but ML-based verdict prediction adds value in three settings: (1)~\\emph{patch correctness prediction}, where a verdict model predicts from a partial test trace whether a candidate patch fixes a bug without running the full suite; (2)~\\emph{flaky test detection}, where trace-based prediction identifies likely-flaky outcomes across runs; and (3)~\\emph{offline trace analysis}, where logged production traces enable retrospective quality assessment without re-execution.\n",
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\nVerdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection.\nException events succeed because they are the runtime's primary fault indicator: error type, stack frame, and error message, packaged in a compact format.\nNon-exception components (variable states, loop iterations, control flow) record \\emph{how} the program ran, not \\emph{whether} it failed.\n\nThis explains three key results.\nFirst, adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit (VOTA $<$ \\texttt{exception\\_only}, Table~\\ref{tab:ablation}), because non-diagnostic content competes for attention.\nSecond, a budget sweep reveals a phase transition at 384$\\to$512 tail tokens (+11.0--22.0pp), matching typical exception traceback length (${\\sim}$400--500 tokens); beyond this threshold, all models converge regardless of scale, with \\texttt{tail\\_2048} capturing 95--98\\% of \\texttt{exception\\_only}'s accuracy.\nThird, the 6.22pp SFT advantage over the best regex baseline concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases (Appendix~\\ref{sec:regex_baselines}), confirming the model learns to distinguish \\emph{whether an exception terminated execution} rather than merely detecting exception presence.\nThe 0.56pp cross-model exception gap and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.\n\n\\paragraph{Why exception\\_only outperforms ae\\_only.}\nAlthough \\texttt{ae\\_only} is a strict superset of the exception signal, multi-seed evaluation reveals that the extra content introduces noise: \\texttt{ae\\_only} achieves 99.64\\%$\\pm$0.49 while \\texttt{exception\\_only} achieves 99.83\\%$\\pm$0.00.\nThe zero-variance result indicates that \\texttt{exception\\_only} captures a minimal sufficient signal, while \\texttt{ae\\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) introduce seed-dependent variance.\n\n\\paragraph{SFT vs.\\ regex: semantic understanding.}\nThe nomarker ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) provides the primary evidence: with all format markers removed, SFT achieves 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96 (Qwen-7B, 3 seeds) and 97.82\\% (Qwen-1.5B), a 4.04pp gap over the best regex baseline (B4, 93.61\\%).\nOn the 8 boundary samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions, SFT correctly classifies 6/8 while the regex misclassifies all 8 (McNemar $p{=}0.041$), confirming that SFT learns to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions.\n\n\\paragraph{Why zero-shot and few-shot prompting fall short.}\nZero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\\% across four models (42.44pp range), while SFT compresses this to 0.56pp.\nThe bottleneck is verdict calibration, not exception detection: models recognize exceptions but cannot distinguish caught from uncaught ones.\nThree-shot ICL (90.84\\%) improves over zero-shot but still trails SFT by 8.99pp, as three examples cannot cover caught-exception diversity.\n\n\\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}\nA regex baseline (B5) achieves 99.33\\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker present in all pass samples, raising the concern that SFT learns this shortcut.\nA \\emph{nomarker} ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:nomarker}) resolves this: removing all markers drops accuracy by only ${\\sim}$2pp (Qwen-7B 97.65\\%$\\pm$0.96, Qwen-1.5B 97.82\\%), and SFT correctly handles 6/8 boundary samples where caught exceptions occur in passing code (vs.\\ 0/8 for the regex).\nThe marker contribution (${\\sim}$9\\%) is small relative to semantic content (${\\sim}$91\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}\nThe 2 errors (samples 901/905, both \\texttt{GeneratorExit} from Python's \\texttt{all()} short-circuit) are shared across most configurations (Appendix~\\ref{sec:error_analysis}).\nCodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\\%, confirming that 99.83\\% is a convergence \\emph{floor}, not a data limitation.\nException-only accuracy is \\emph{signal-limited} rather than \\emph{capacity-limited}: three families (1.5B--13B) converge on the same floor, while \\texttt{no\\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\\% $\\to$ 75.1\\% $\\to$ 76.5\\%).\n\n\\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency.}\nCodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\\sim}$20\\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical inputs, reducing the verdict label's loss share to ${\\sim}$0.085\\%.\nA label-only loss variant recovers CodeLlama to 98.2\\% at tail-1024 but collapses at tail-2048 (41.8\\%), indicating LoRA long-sequence instability (Appendix~\\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).\nTokenizer efficiency is a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training.\n\n\\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}\nThe two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\\geq}$99\\%; Tier~2 = 86.1\\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.\nFirst, it implies a \\emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may degrade performance through attention dilution.\nSecond, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised. Even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).\nThird, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (median 150 tokens vs.\\ ${\\sim}$1{,}900 for VOTA post-truncation) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).\n\n\\paragraph{Practical applications.}\nTest frameworks report pass/fail, but ML-based verdict prediction adds value in three settings: (1)~\\emph{patch correctness prediction}, where a verdict model predicts from a partial test trace whether a candidate patch fixes a bug without running the full suite; (2)~\\emph{flaky test detection}, where trace-based prediction identifies likely-flaky outcomes across runs; and (3)~\\emph{offline trace analysis}, where logged production traces enable retrospective quality assessment without re-execution.\n",
```
